title: How to Unclog a Toilet Without Calling a Plumber
hook: A clogged toilet always seems to happen at the worst possible moment. The good news is that most of the time you can clear it yourself in about ten minutes, with no plumber and no harsh chemicals. Here are the seven steps, and what to do if nothing works.
intro: Most toilet clogs sit in the first bend of the drain, just out of sight, and they are made of too much paper or something that should never have been flushed. That is why pressure, soap and a simple cable are usually enough. We will start with the gentlest method and work up, so you never do more than you need to.
youNeedNarration: Here is what you will need. A flange plunger. A pair of rubber gloves. Dish soap. A bucket of hot tap water. A toilet auger for the stubborn cases. And a few old towels for the floor.

steps.title: Stop the water first
steps.narration: Step one. If the bowl is filling up, do not flush again. A second flush sends a full tank, at least a gallon and a half of water, into a bowl that has nowhere to drain. Lift the lid off the tank and push the rubber flapper down over the hole at the bottom. That stops more water from entering the bowl. Then reach behind the toilet and turn the shut-off valve clockwise until it stops. Now the water level cannot rise, and you can work without a flood.
steps.tip: No flush until the clog is gone
steps.mistake: Flushing a second time to see if it clears

steps.title: Protect the floor and gear up
steps.narration: Step two. Lay old towels or newspaper around the base of the toilet. Pull on a pair of rubber gloves, and open a window if you can. If the bowl is full to the brim, bail some water into a bucket until it is about half full. You want enough water to cover the plunger, but not enough to splash over the rim.
steps.tip: Half a bowl of water is ideal
steps.mistake: Plunging a bowl that is full to the brim

steps.title: Seal the drain with a flange plunger
steps.narration: Step three. Use a flange plunger, the kind with a soft rubber sleeve sticking out of the cup. A flat sink plunger cannot seal the curved drain of a toilet. Run the plunger under hot water for a minute so the rubber softens. For an even tighter seal, smear a little petroleum jelly around the rim of the cup. Lower it in at an angle to let the air escape, then fit the sleeve into the drain hole. Make your first push slow and gentle, so trapped air does not blast water back at you.
steps.mistake: Using a flat sink plunger on a toilet

steps.title: Plunge in a steady rhythm
steps.narration: Step four. Keep the seal and pump the handle straight up and down, fifteen to twenty times. Push firmly, but pull just as hard, because the suction does half the work. The cup must stay under water the whole time, so top up the bowl from your bucket if the level gets low. On the last stroke, yank the plunger up sharply to break the seal. If the water rushes down the drain, the clog has moved. If nothing changes, repeat the whole round two or three more times before moving on.
steps.tip: Pull as hard as you push
steps.mistake: Breaking the seal on every stroke

steps.title: Loosen it with dish soap and hot water
steps.narration: Step five. Squirt about half a cup of dish soap into the bowl. No dish soap? Shampoo or liquid hand soap works the same way. Fill a bucket with hot tap water, hot but never boiling, because boiling water can crack porcelain. Pour it in from waist height, so the weight of the water pushes on the clog. Wait fifteen to twenty minutes while the soap lubricates the pipe. If the water level has dropped while you waited, that is a very good sign: the clog is already letting water through. Then plunge again, and most stubborn clogs give up at this point.
steps.tip: Hot from the tap, never boiling

steps.title: Break it up with a toilet auger
steps.narration: Step six. For a clog that still will not move, use a toilet auger, also called a closet auger. Its rubber sleeve protects the porcelain from scratches. The cable is about three feet long, enough to reach any clog inside the toilet itself. Rest the curved end in the drain and feed the cable in by turning the crank clockwise. When you feel resistance, keep cranking gently to break the clog apart or hook it. Then wind the cable back out slowly and drop whatever comes up into the bucket.
steps.mistake: Using a wire coat hanger instead

steps.title: Test the flush and clean up
steps.narration: Step seven. Turn the shut-off valve back on and let the tank refill. Take the lid off and keep one hand near the flapper, ready to close it. Flush once and watch the bowl empty with a strong swirl. If the water rises instead, close the flapper right away and go back to the auger. Then flush three or four sheets of toilet paper as a final test: if they vanish, the drain is truly clear. Finish by rinsing the plunger and auger in the clean flush water, then disinfect them, the floor and the handle.
steps.tip: Keep a hand near the flapper
steps.mistake: Walking away before the test flush

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Now, the mistakes that turn a small clog into a big problem. One, flushing again and again, which is how bathrooms flood. Two, pouring in chemical drain cleaner. It rarely works on toilets, it can damage the pipes, and if you plunge afterwards it can splash onto your skin. Three, using boiling water, which can crack the bowl. And four, poking around with a wire coat hanger, which scratches the porcelain for good.

recap.narration: Let's run through it one more time. Stop the water. Protect the floor. Seal the drain with a flange plunger. Plunge in a steady rhythm. Add dish soap and hot water. Bring in the auger. Then test the flush and clean up. If it still will not clear, give it a night. If other drains are backing up too, call a plumber. And from now on, wipes go in the trash.

outro: That's how you unclog a toilet without calling a plumber. If this saved your day, subscribe to WikiTube for a new how-to every day, and tell us in the comments what you want us to explain next.

metadata.title: How to Unclog a Toilet Fast (7 Steps, No Plumber)
metadata.description: A clogged toilet is usually a 10-minute fix. In this video you'll learn the 7 steps to unclog a toilet yourself: stop the water, protect the floor, seal the drain with a flange plunger, plunge in rhythm, use dish soap and hot water, break the clog with a toilet auger, then test the flush. Plus what to try when nothing works, the 4 signs that mean you should call a plumber, how to keep it from clogging again, and the 4 mistakes to avoid.

short.hook: Toilet clogged? Do not flush again. Three steps, about ten minutes.

steps.title: Stop the water
steps.narration: One. Push the flapper down in the tank and close the valve behind the toilet.

steps.title: Plunge with a flange plunger
steps.narration: Two. Seal the drain with a flange plunger and pump fifteen to twenty times.

steps.title: Dish soap + hot water
steps.narration: Three. Still stuck? Half a cup of dish soap, a bucket of hot tap water, wait fifteen minutes, plunge again.

bonus.label: STILL STUCK?
bonus.title: Two last things to try
bonus.narration: Still stuck? Before you give up, there are two more things worth trying. The first one is time. A paper clog softens by itself, so leave the soap and hot water in the bowl overnight, and plunge again in the morning. The second one is a wet and dry shop vacuum, if you own one, and never a regular household vacuum. Vacuum the water out of the bowl, wrap an old towel around the hose to seal the drain, and let the suction pull the clog back out. As for baking soda and vinegar, the fizz looks impressive, but on a solid clog it does far less than soap, hot water and a good plunger.

bonus.label: CALL A PRO
bonus.title: When to call a plumber
bonus.narration: Sometimes the problem is not in your toilet at all, and that is when you stop and call a plumber. Sign number one: when you flush, water comes up in the shower or the bathtub. Sign number two: several drains in the house are slow or gurgling at the same time. Both mean the blockage is in the main sewer line, far beyond the reach of a plunger. Sign number three: you know a hard object went down, like a toy, a toothbrush or a phone. Forcing it can wedge it deeper. And sign number four: the same toilet clogs every few days, which points to a deeper problem that a pro should look at.
bonus.tip: Several slow drains mean the main line

bonus.label: PREVENTION
bonus.title: Keep it from clogging again
bonus.narration: Finally, here is how to never need this video again. Only two things belong in a toilet: toilet paper and human waste. Wipes, even the ones sold as flushable, do not break down like paper. Put them in the trash, along with cotton pads, dental floss and paper towels. When you use a lot of paper, flush twice: once halfway through, and once at the end. If you have young children, a simple lid lock keeps toys out of the bowl. And keep that flange plunger next to the toilet, so the next clog is a two-minute job.
bonus.tip: When in doubt, put it in the trash
